title: UK Autumn Budget: Key takeaways

# UK Autumn Budget: Key takeaways


Nick Bearne, Fraser Holmes-Mackay and Louise Towers from the Wealth Advisory team; Luke Mayberry, Investment Strategist


28 October 2026


**Share this Insight**

Please note: The article does not constitute advice or any form of recommendation. Barclays Private Bank and Wealth Management does not offer tax advice, and professional advice should always be sought.


In the first Budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham MP, Chancellor John Healey MP unveiled the UK government’s tax and spending plans. As expected, it was a relatively low-drama Budget, with few major surprises and some of the more difficult spending decisions left for the 2027 Spending Review. The initial reaction from financial markets has also been subdued.


Here we outline some of the key changes ahead that may affect wealth holders, what remains unchanged and how financial markets have reacted.


## A difficult balancing act


The UK economy has proved more resilient than expected this year, despite tighter financial conditions and geopolitical uncertainty. However, higher oil and gas prices following the escalation of conflict in the Middle East have added to inflation pressures and complicated the outlook for interest rates.


Higher borrowing costs and debt interest payments have also reduced the government’s fiscal headroom. Faced with the challenge of supporting the economy while maintaining fiscal credibility, the Chancellor opted against sweeping changes to the tax system, instead announcing a series of more targeted measures. On spending, the focus was on near-term support to ease cost-of-living pressures, alongside continued investment in housing, infrastructure and public services.


## Key changes for wealth holders


**New tax relief for business founders**
The government announced a new Founders’ Relief, offering qualifying founders a 10% capital gains tax (CGT) rate on up to £10 million of qualifying lifetime gains. However, some of the detail is still to be confirmed through a technical consultation, including who will qualify as a founder. For business owners considering an exit, these details will be important when assessing the timing or structure of a sale.


**Tax rises on property and savings income**
From 6 April 2027, the tax rates applying to both property and savings income will rise to 24% for basic-rate taxpayers, 44% for higher-rate taxpayers and 49% for additional-rate taxpayers. The increase announced at this Budget comes on top of the two-percentage-point rise announced at last year’s Autumn Budget, meaning the rates will ultimately be four percentage points higher. For those with significant property or savings income, the changes may prompt a review of how assets are held, including available allowances and tax-efficient wrappers.


**Business Asset Disposal Relief reduced**
The lifetime limit for gains eligible for Business Asset Disposal Relief will fall from £1 million to £500,000 from 6 April 2027, potentially increasing the tax payable by business owners on a qualifying disposal. The government estimates that, despite the reduction, three-quarters of claimants will continue to receive relief on their entire gain. Business owners contemplating a sale may also need to consider the change alongside the new Founders’ Relief outlined above.


**Cash ISA limit retained**
The government has dropped plans to reduce the amount savers can put into cash ISAs, retaining the £20,000 annual ISA limit from 6 April 2027. With tax on savings income due to rise from April 2027, making appropriate use of tax-efficient wrappers may become increasingly important.


The government will also work with the investment industry on a new ISA incentive for people investing in a stocks and shares ISA for the first time. This is part of the government’s wider initiative to encourage more savers to consider investing. The detailed design has yet to be developed.


## Changes still to take effect


Several previously announced changes are due to affect wealth holders in the next few years.


**Pensions in scope for inheritance tax**


There were no new changes to inheritance tax (IHT) rules, but from 6 April 2027, unused pension savings will be included in the value of an individual's estate for IHT purposes. Pensions may therefore need to be considered alongside other assets when thinking about inheritance planning. As a reminder, there is no IHT payable on the first £325,000 of an estate’s value. This threshold will remain frozen until April 2031.


**Making Tax Digital threshold lowered**


The rollout of Making Tax Digital for Income Tax is continuing. Since 6 April 2026, most sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £50,000 have been required to keep digital records and provide quarterly updates to HMRC using compatible software. The threshold will fall to £30,000 from 6 April 2027 and £20,000 from 6 April 2028, bringing more individuals with self-employment or property income into the regime.


**Mansion tax on properties over £2 million**


A previously announced annual levy on properties valued at over £2 million will take effect from 6 April 2028. Despite speculation ahead of the Budget that the threshold could be reduced to £1.5 million, it remains unchanged. The High Value Council Tax Surcharge will start at £2,500 for properties worth between £2 million and £2.5 million, rising across four bands to £7,500 for properties worth more than £5 million. Charges will increase annually in line with CPI inflation from 2029-30 onwards.


**Changes to ‘salary sacrifice’ pension contributions**


From 6 April 2029, a £2,000 annual limit will be introduced on the amount employees can save into their pensions under a ‘salary sacrifice’ scheme without paying national insurance (NI). Employees will pay the full NI rate on contributions above that limit, namely 8% on earnings under £50,000 and 2% on any income above this threshold. This is most likely to affect higher earners making substantial pension contributions through salary or bonus exchange.


## What has not changed


Several key areas of the tax system were left unchanged, including the ‘big three’ – non-savings income tax, employee's national insurance and VAT – as pledged in the Labour Party’s pre-election manifesto.


**Capital gains tax**


Raising capital gains tax (CGT) was one of the most widely discussed options ahead of the Budget, but the Chancellor opted against changing the headline rates. CGT rates remain at 18% for basic rate taxpayers, and 24% for higher earners. The annual personal allowance also remains frozen at £3,000 for individuals (per tax year) and £1,500 for trusts.


**Income tax and national insurance**


Income tax and national insurance thresholds remain frozen until 2031. While not an explicit tax increase, freezing thresholds can result in more people moving into higher tax brackets as their incomes rise. Income tax rates remain unchanged, with 20% tax payable on income between £12,571 and £50,270; 40% on earnings between £50,271 and £125,140; and 45% tax payable thereafter.


**Tax on dividends**


Having been raised at last year’s Autumn Budget, dividend tax rates remain unchanged at 10.75% at the basic rate, 35.75% at the higher rate, and 39.35% at the additional rate. The annual tax-free allowance on dividend income remains at £500.


## How have markets reacted?


The initial market reaction to the Budget has been relatively muted, suggesting that investors are broadly comfortable with the fiscal outlook so far. Gilts had been closely watched ahead of the announcement. The domestic fiscal risk premium had already diminished materially in the weeks leading up to the Budget, with the long end of the gilt curve outperforming as investors grew more confident that Healey would avoid a significant unfunded stimulus package. So far, that confidence appears to have been justified, with the government maintaining a buffer against its fiscal rules and gilt yields moving only modestly. Sterling has also remained relatively stable.


The reaction from UK equities has also been subdued, although the impact has varied across sectors. Limited movement in gilt yields has helped cushion the immediate impact on rate-sensitive sectors such as real estate and utilities. Shares in UK banks rose after John Healey announced that tax increases on the sector would be smaller than expected and temporary. More broadly, there has been limited movement at the index level so far, with the FTSE 100’s high international revenue exposure providing some insulation from changes in domestic fiscal policy.


## Looking ahead


While there were no major surprises in today’s announcement, a Budget can be an opportune time to revisit financial plans and ensure you are prepared for the changes ahead. This might include looking again at the allowances and structures available to you, as part of a broader review of how your wealth is managed. As ever, it’s important to assess any changes in the context of your individual circumstances and long-term objectives. With tax rules both complex and evolving, seeking professional advice can help you make informed decisions and help you plan the future you want.
